title: SLO-driven Burst Orchestrator and Latency Smoothing — PRD Brief
content:
Context:
This brief proposes a focused PRD for an SLO-driven Burst Orchestrator (SBO) for Dedicated pools. The goal is to give customers predictable latency SLOs while enabling short-term burst capacity and strong tenant isolation. This doc is intentionally compact — it captures the problem, proposed end-to-end behavior, key components, simulation plan, rollout guardrails, and open questions for engineering and SRE to iterate on.

Problem statement:
Teams buying Dedicated capacity need two competing guarantees: (1) predictable latency (p99/p95) for critical requests, and (2) economically efficient use of idle GPU for opportunistic bursts. Existing autoscaling and burst designs either favor full throughput (at cost) or degrade latency under contention. We need a control plane that makes bursts conditional on SLO headroom and that enforces isolation policies without manual tenant intervention.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Maintain latency SLOs for reserve-backed requests: p95 <= target_latency and p99 degradation <= 2x baseline under normal load (target_latency set per-customer).
- Allow short bursts (1–10m) up to X% of idle capacity with an explicit cost model and failback to lower-cost model variants when headroom is low.
- Prevent noisy-tenant impact: limit cross-tenant tail latency spikes to <5% increased p99 for neighbors during bursts.
- Automated decisioning: SBO makes deterministic burst accept/reject decisions based on telemetry and declared policies; manual override for ops.
- Observability: dashboard with real-time headroom, queued requests, burst tokens consumed, and per-tenant tail-latency delta.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not design billing mechanics for bursts (billing is handled by pricing team separately).
- SBO will not change model weights or quantization; it can select pre-configured model variants only.

Key concepts and terminology:
- Headroom: the observable capacity margin compared to the capacity required to meet latency SLO across reserved lanes (computed from queue lengths, per-token latencies, and active slots).
- Burst Token: a short-lived credit consumed to allow a set of requests to execute using idle capacity. Tokens have TTL (configurable) and cost weight.
- SLO Window: moving window used to compute whether latency SLOs are currently satisfied (default 5m).
- Soft Isolation: throttles/limits that reduce cross-tenant interference without hard-preempting running batches.

User stories:
- As an enterprise tenant, I want my latency SLO guaranteed even when other tenants burst, so my customer-facing endpoints stay responsive.
- As a dev on a high-throughput app, I want to request burst credits for a sudden spike and have the system grant short bursts if headroom exists — otherwise fallback predictably.
- As an operator, I want clear signals and a runbook when bursts cause SLO churn so I can troubleshoot and escalate.

Behavioral design (end-to-end):
1) Admission: incoming requests tagged with tenant_id + priority + desired SLA lane. SBO computes available headroom across the pool within the SLO window. If safe_headroom >= requested_cost, grant immediate execution using burst tokens; otherwise, check fallback policies (queue, route to lower-cost model, or reject with explicit error).
2) Enforcement: while bursting, SBO continuously monitors tail latencies. If p99 across reserved lanes exceeds threshold, SBO will first throttle non-reserved burst flows using weighted fair queuing, then revoke lowest-priority burst tokens.
3) Graceful revocation: in-flight tokens are marked for no-new-requests and expire naturally; short-running tasks get to finish. For long-running streaming calls, SBO negotiates a fall-through to lower-resource model variant or returns a transient capacity-unavailable response.
4) Isolation fences: SBO supports soft fences (rate caps, per-tenant concurrent limit) and hard fences (preemption of opportunistic workloads) configurable per-customer.

Component breakdown:
- Admission Controller: lightweight service collates telemetry and makes grant decisions; exposes gRPC/REST endpoints for routers.
- Headroom Estimator: streaming job that synthesizes queue depth, active batch sizes, and kernel latency profiles into a single headroom metric per-pool.
- Token Ledger: durable store for burst tokens with issuance, consumption, and decay semantics; supports audits.
- Enforcement Hooks (runtime): small runtime client integrated into serving runtime to implement throttles, per-request tagging, and model-variant routing when revoking.
- Dashboard & Alerts: headroom timeline, token consumption heatmap, per-tenant latency deltas, runbook links.

Simulation and validation plan (must be executed before beta):
- Synthetic generator: traffic generator that can produce mixed-priority workloads and configurable bursts.
- Replay harness: replay real traffic traces from opt-in customers (anonymized) to validate headroom model accuracy.
- A/B tests in staging: compare current autoscaler vs SBO with metrics: SLO miss rate, cost-per-token, opportunity utilization, neighbor p99 delta.
- Chaos tests: sudden node loss and delayed kernel responses to validate graceful revocation logic.

SLOs and success metrics:
- Primary: p95 under normal load meets target_latency for reserved lanes 99.9% of time in test runs.
- Secondary: p99 tail increase for neighbors during bursts <= 5% relative.
- Utilization: average opportunistic utilization improved by 20% vs baseline without increasing SLO misses.
- Cost: burst decisions should not increase per-token cost by more than 10% for reserved workloads.

Operational runbook (short):
- Alert: p95 SLO breach + headroom < 0 for >2m -> page SRE on-call.
- Initial steps: check token ledger consumption; examine recent admission decisions; if token storm, disable automated granting and allow manual grants.
- Containment: enable hard fences for top offending tenants; scale up reserved capacity if persistent.
- Postmortem: capture token issuance timeline, headroom estimator logs, and enforcement hook traces.

Rollout plan and guardrails:
- Phase 0 (lab): unit tests + simulation harness, headroom estimator validated vs historical traces.
- Phase 1 (staging): SBO in passive mode (decisions only) for two weeks; compare decisions to current behavior.
- Phase 2 (limited beta): enable grants for a small set of internal and friendly-customer tenants with conservative TTL and per-tenant cap.
- Phase 3 (wider beta): expand to <20% of pools; add automated throttling; monitor metrics and runbook ops load.
- Phase 4 (GA): opt-in for all customers with UI to configure soft/hard fences and burst budgets.

Security, compliance, and audit:
- Token ledger must be write-audited and exportable for compliance reviews.
- Admission decisions are deterministic and recorded for at least 90 days for billing/forensics.

Open questions / risks:
- Headroom model accuracy: how to tune estimator for varying kernel mixes (Llama vs Mistral)? Need per-model calibration dataset.
- Billing alignment: how to represent transient burst consumption in invoices without confusing customers? (work with pricing).
- Complexity vs benefit: SBO introduces several moving parts; can we iterate with a minimal MVP (admission + tokens + enforcement hooks) and postpone fancy estimation?
- Support burden: anticipate increased ops noise during initial rollout; require a dedicated on-call run for 2 weeks after limited beta.

Next steps (near-term):
- Align on MVP scope (Nadia + Rafael + infra lead) by 2025-11-12.
- Implementation spike: Headroom Estimator + Admission Controller prototype (2 sprints).
- Build synthetic replay harness and run baseline experiments (owner: applied-ml).
- Draft SLA/contract language for burst options with pricing (work with go-to-market).

Appendix: quick API sketch (informal)
- POST /admit { tenant_id, priority, tokens_requested, model_variant, request_weight } -> { granted: bool, token_id, ttl, reason }
- GET /headroom?pool_id -> { headroom_pct, estimated_safe_requests }
- Webhook: /enforcement/revoked { token_id, reason }

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working PRD brief; please comment on the headroom estimator assumptions and the proposed graceful revocation approach. Ops should weigh in on the runbook and paging thresholds. Product and pricing must align on whether burst tokens are free, prepaid, or billed post-fact.

-- end of brief --
